sentences.text: Net income grew from $5.89 billion in FY2016 [F21] to $7.57 billion in FY2025 [F30], a 2.8% CAGR [F117], while net interest income compounded at 4.0% [F115].
Net income was volatile around that path: down 28.3% in FY2020 to $4.96 billion [D99][F25], up 60.6% in FY2021 to $7.96 billion [D125][F26], then down 26.8% in FY2022 [D151].
The FY2021 rise reflected a lower provision, which the filing ties to improved economic conditions and credit performance [P57], moving from $3.81 billion in FY2020 [X140] to -$1.17 billion [X141].
The FY2022 fall followed a provision that rose to $1.98 billion [X142], which the filing links to the MUB acquisition and related balance sheet actions [P36].
Bank revenue grew 4.4% to $28.5 billion in FY2025 [D239][D219], led by noninterest income up 7.6% to $11.9 billion [D235][F20].
Noninterest income rose on higher payment services revenue, from merchant processing and card revenue driven by sales volume, and on trust fees [P11].
Payment Services added 1.4pp to FY2025 growth [D261] from a 25.8% revenue share [D259], while Consumer and Business Banking subtracted 1.3pp [D253].
Net interest income rose 2.2% to $16.6 billion [D234][F10] on loan growth, fixed asset repricing and lower rates paid on deposits [P16].
Per-share growth outpaced net income: EPS rose 21.9% to $4.62 [D228][F40] against 20.2% net income growth [D227], with diluted shares down 0.2% [D237].
The efficiency ratio was 59.0% in FY2025 [D220], just below its 59.3% window median [D277] and the banks peer median of 61.7% [D281].
The ratio peaked at 67.4% in FY2023 [D276], then eased to 62.9% in FY2024 [D195] and 59.0% in FY2025 [D220].
The FY2023 peak came from a 26.6% rise in noninterest expense to $18.9 billion [D188][X133], which the filing ties to merger costs, MUB operating expenses and the FDIC special assessment [P30].
Expense fell 8.9% in FY2024 [D213] on lower merger and FDIC charges [P17], then 2.0% to $16.8 billion in FY2025 [D238][X135] on lower compensation [P10].
The provision was 7.7% of FY2025 revenue [D221], above the banks peer median of 6.1% [D285] and the 6.3% of FY2016 [D7].
For a bank, operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings measure, so capital return is the better test.
Buybacks and dividends totalled $3.66 billion in FY2025 [D218][F30], or 48.3% of net income of $7.57 billion [D218][F30].
Dividends paid rose to $3.17 billion [X95] while buybacks fell to $489 million [X85] from $4.53 billion in FY2019 [X79].
Operating cash flow was $7.97 billion in FY2025 [F60], down 29.8% [D230]; the filings cited do not explain that move.
Shareholders' equity rose 11.3% to $65.2 billion in FY2025 [D233][F114], while loans were 73.5% of deposits [D224], down from 80.5% in FY2016 [D10].
Return on average equity of 12.2% [D226] ranked at the 71st percentile of seven bank peers, against a peer median of 11.8% [D282][D283].
Cash and equivalents fell 17.0% to $46.9 billion [D232][F97]; long-term debt is not in the pack after FY2022 [F104], so FY2025 net debt cannot be computed.
Debt issued of $10.4 billion exceeded debt repaid of $9.05 billion in FY2025 [X105][X115].
[R1] Bank revenue fell 2.4% in FY2024 to $27.3 billion [R1][D214][D194], driven by a 6.4% drop in net interest income [D209] that the filing ties to higher deposit rates [P20].
The decline did not persist, as revenue recovered 4.4% in FY2025 [D239].
Reserves were built rather than released: the allowance rose to 2.0% of loans [D225] from 1.6% in FY2016 [D11].
The provision fell to $2.19 billion from $2.24 billion [X145][X144] on improved credit quality, though net charge-offs rose [P12].
Efficiency ratio: a return above the FY2024 level of 62.9% [D195] would reverse FY2025's cost gains and would appear in the FY2026 10-K.
Provision as a share of revenue: a fall below the FY2016 level of 6.3% [D7], from 7.7% [D221], would confirm the credit trend in the FY2026 10-K.
Return on average equity: a fall below FY2024's 11.1% [D201] would reverse the FY2025 gain and leave it under the 11.8% peer median [D283].
